newsitem.title: UK: Stressed Britons appreciate trade unions -TUC.
newsitem.headline: Stressed Britons appreciate trade unions -TUC.

text.p: British people are feeling increasingly stressed and insecure at work, and trade unions have won back their popularity as a result, according to two surveys conducted for the Trades Union Congress (TUC).
A survey of 7,000 health and safety representatives found that 68 percent felt stress was the biggest hazards in their workplace.

A separate NOP survey of 1,499 people -- split roughly equally between unionists, non-unionists and people not in work -- found that 57 percent were more insecure than two years ago, and 55 percent expected their work to become even more insecure in the years ahead.
One in three felt too afraid to take time off when sick and often felt obliged to work late.
As a result, 80 percent of people agreed that unions provided vital protection for many groups of workers.
The TUC is holding its annual conference from Monday, and a main theme will be rights at work.
The unions were highly unpopular in the 1970s and 1980s and the Conservative government used that to push through a series of laws to reduce their powers.
Now, according to the NOP poll, only 17 percent of Britons feel all the restrictions were right and should stay.
Some 56 percent said the Conservatives were right to introduce some reforms, but had gone too far.
TUC general secretary John Monks told a news conference the poll "nails the lie that trade unions are seen as historic relics."

"The poll shows that people are fed up of being taken for granted at work. They have been put under greater and greater pressure, expected to work harder and longer than ever before, but then discarded at the first sign of any difficulty," he said.
